concepts.name: Clarify and agree an approach before coding
Talking through your reasoning the whole time
Testing your own code before saying it's done
Timed practice and reviewing a recording

questions.prompt: The interviewer has just read out a medium problem. According to the Tech Interview Handbook's cheatsheet, what should you do first?

choices.text: Start typing a brute-force solution so you have something working
Repeat the question in your own words and ask about input size, range and edge cases
Ask the interviewer which data structure they expect
Think silently until you have the optimal solution

questions.explanation: The cheatsheet's first step is to paraphrase the question back and clarify it: how big the input is, what range the values have, whether there can be negatives, duplicates or empty input, and to work a small example. Starting to code before that risks solving the wrong problem, and thinking in silence gives the interviewer nothing to grade.

questions.prompt: When does the Tech Interview Handbook's cheatsheet say you should start writing code?

choices.text: As soon as you understand the question, to save time for testing
Once you have written pseudocode for the whole solution on the board
Only once you have found the optimal solution to the problem
After you explain your approach and complexity and the interviewer agrees

questions.explanation: The cheatsheet says to explain a few approaches at a high level, discuss their trade-offs, state their time and space complexity, agree on one, and only code after the interviewer gives you the green light. It also asks for real, working code rather than pseudocode. A brute force you have agreed on is a fine place to start.

questions.prompt: You have 30 minutes for a medium problem. What do you do in the first few minutes, before writing code, and why isn't that time wasted?

model_answer.summary: Restate the problem, clarify inputs and edge cases, work a small example, and agree an approach with its complexity; it prevents solving the wrong problem and is part of what you are graded on.
key_points: Paraphrase the question back to the interviewer
Ask about input size and value range, and about empty input, negatives and duplicates
Work through a small example by hand to check you understood
Describe one or more approaches with their time and space complexity, and agree on one before coding
Interviewers grade communication and problem solving as well as code, so this time earns credit and saves rewriting later

questions.explanation: Under time pressure it feels safer to start typing, but a wrong assumption found after 20 minutes of code costs far more than 3 minutes of questions. The Tech Interview Handbook's rubric rewards asking good clarifying questions and working systematically, so the planning is visible evidence, not overhead.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour does the Tech Interview Handbook's coding interview rubric mark down under communication?

choices.text: Asking clarifying questions before starting
Starting with a brute-force approach before optimising
Jumping into coding without explaining the approach
Stating the time and space complexity out loud

questions.explanation: The rubric's strong signals include constantly communicating, even while coding, and it marks down jumping into coding without explaining and staying silent even when the interviewer speaks to you. Clarifying questions and stated complexity are things it rewards, and a brute force you explain first is a normal way to begin.

questions.prompt: Ten minutes into a problem you are stuck on how to avoid visiting cells twice. What is the best thing to do?

choices.text: Talk through what you've tried and what's blocking you, so the interviewer can steer
Go quiet so you can concentrate, and only speak again once you have the full answer
Ask the interviewer to tell you the solution, so you can save time for coding
Switch to a different approach silently, without telling the interviewer

questions.explanation: The interviewer can only credit reasoning they can hear, and the rubric asks for constant communication. Talking through the blocker shows how you work on problems and gives the interviewer a chance to offer a small hint. Going silent looks like being stuck with no plan, and asking for the whole answer gives away the problem-solving marks.

questions.prompt: Why should you talk out loud during a coding interview, and what exactly should you be saying while you write code?

model_answer.summary: Communication is one of the areas you are graded on and the interviewer can only credit what they hear, so narrate your approach, your reasons and trade-offs, and what each part of the code does.
key_points: The rubric grades communication alongside problem solving, technical competency and testing
The interviewer can't see your reasoning unless you say it, so silent good thinking earns little
Before coding: your approach, why you chose it, its trade-offs and complexity
While coding: what the current piece is for, such as 'this set records cells I've already queued'
Talking lets the interviewer correct a wrong direction early, before you spend the time

questions.explanation: Thinking out loud turns your process into evidence. It also protects you: when a bug appears, an interviewer who followed your plan can see it is a slip, not a misunderstanding. That is why this Lesson's drill has you talk the whole time, even alone.

questions.prompt: You have just finished writing your solution. According to the Tech Interview Handbook's cheatsheet, what comes next?

choices.text: Tell the interviewer you are done and wait for their feedback on it
Ask the interviewer to run your code against their hidden tests
Rewrite the whole solution from scratch in a cleaner, more idiomatic style
Scan for bugs, step through edge-case tests, and restate the complexity

questions.explanation: The cheatsheet's testing step is to scan the code for mistakes, brainstorm edge cases with the interviewer, step through the code with those cases, look for places to refactor, and restate the time and space complexity. Declaring 'done' without testing leaves the rubric's testing area empty, and finding your own bugs counts in your favour.

questions.prompt: You have solved Number of Islands. Which set of test cases does the most to show your code is correct?

choices.text: The two examples from the problem statement, run twice to be sure
All water, one land cell, an island on the edges, and islands touching diagonally
One very large random grid, to check that it runs fast enough
Grids made entirely of land, in several sizes up to the 300 × 300 limit

questions.explanation: Good tests cover the corners where code breaks: no islands at all, the smallest input, cells on the boundary (bounds checks), and the diagonal case that tests 4-directional connection. The given examples are a start, not proof. A large random grid is hard to check by hand, and all-land grids only test one shape.

questions.prompt: You record yourself solving two medium problems in 60 minutes while talking out loud. When you watch it back, what is most worth checking?

choices.text: Each rubric area: silences, coding before explaining, pacing, untested bugs
How fast you typed and finished compared with your last recording
Whether your code matches the NeetCode reference solution line for line
Whether you used the most advanced data structure available to you

questions.explanation: A recording shows what an interviewer sees, so review it against what they grade: communication, problem solving, clean working code and testing. Look for silent stretches, jumping into code, time overruns (about 30 minutes per medium in this drill) and bugs that testing would have caught. Typing speed and matching a reference solution are not what you are graded on.

questions.prompt: Plan your 60-minute timed drill of two medium problems, then say how you would use the recording to decide what to practise next.

model_answer.summary: Give each problem about 30 minutes split into clarify, plan, code and test, talk the whole time, then review the recording against the rubric and turn the weak spots into the next problems to redo.
key_points: Budget about 30 minutes per problem, and move on when the time is up
Within each problem: clarify, agree an approach with its complexity, code, then test and restate the complexity
Talk out loud throughout, as in a real interview
Watching back, check each rubric area: communication, problem solving, technical competency and testing
Write down specific weak spots, such as long silences or a missed edge case, and pick problems that practise them for your next redo

questions.explanation: Timed practice builds the pacing a real interview needs, and the recording gives you an honest view of it. The review only helps if it ends in something specific to practise, which is why the Lesson pairs the drill with redoing the problems you found hardest.
